bull_bear.body:
- Dual financial-and-physical capability: management identifies the ability to operate simultaneously across derivatives markets (MCX, NCDEX, COMEX, IIBX) and physical procurement/delivery infrastructure as its core competitive advantage in a volatile market
- Structural procurement cost advantage: GIFT City Qualified Jeweller status and India-UAE CEPA Tariff Rate Quota access enable duty-concessional gold imports through IIBX, which the Company describes as a cost advantage over peers reliant on traditional nominated bank channels
- Early-mover institutional position at IIBX as India's bullion import architecture formalises, which management says creates lasting structural value as SBI and other PSUs join as participants
- Counterparty risk record: the Company states it navigated the most volatile precious metals environment in a generation without a single counterparty default, with every transaction fully hedged and physically backed
- Approved risk-management mechanism with strict limits on maximum exposure, stop loss and maximum deal size, hedging via exchange-traded futures and options; 100% of disclosed domestic agri-commodity exposures (coriander, guar gum, guar seeds) were hedged through exchange derivatives
- Established trading relationships: trusted position across India's bullion corridors, and for AJL, associations with major bullion bankers plus a strong net worth and robust banking relationships that support the Group's trading fund-raising requirements
- Diversified portfolio across agri commodities, bullion, base metals, derivatives, equity markets and bespoke jewellery, reducing reliance on any single market segment
- Design-led premium jewellery positioning: handcrafted designs and trusted supply relationships in the premium/bespoke segment, where management says design innovation, artisan craftsmanship and brand trust command a price premium with greater resilience to commodity price volatility
- Board independence: over fifty percent of the Board comprises Independent Directors, including one Woman Independent Director, and an independent internal audit firm reports directly to the Audit Committee
- A decade of disciplined execution and institutional relationship-building under current management since 2015 (management's own characterisation)
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Bullion price concentration risk — Management flags that bullion trading constitutes the substantial majority of AEL's revenues, so a sustained correction in precious metals prices or spread compression could disproportionately impact financial performance. This is a structural single-commodity concentration, not a cyclical one.
- Working capital intensity at scale — Listed as a threat: margin management, collateral management and reconciliation demands are materially different from two years prior following the step-up in trading scale, and technology and treasury systems must continue to scale commensurately.
- Treasury and risk-management infrastructure must scale with volumes — The MD&A 'Risk and Concerns' section states the scale of treasury operations requires continued investment in risk management infrastructure as volumes compound — an ongoing cost and operational-failure exposure tied to growth.
- Lending vertical undercapitalised relative to the opportunity — Management states the lending vertical requires capital scale-up to capture the full opportunity and that internal accruals alone may not sustain the target growth rate — implying a dependence on external capital.
- Middle East conflict — energy and macro risk — The Strait of Hormuz disruption removes a significant share of global crude supply and the US waiver for Russian crude purchases expired April 11, 2026. Management warns this could drive imported inflation, weaken the rupee and force the RBI to pause its easing cycle, while higher oil prices raise operating costs for commodity transportation, storage and processing across AEL's supply chain.
- Extreme commodity price volatility and intraday dislocation — FY 2025-26 saw gold and silver at generational highs and one of the most violent intraday reversals in modern commodity history (silver, December 29, 2025). Management cites the flash crash as demonstrating the risks of volatile commodity markets; the derivatives desk operated in the most demanding environment in the Company's history.
- Multi-exchange, cross-border operational and control complexity — Operations span MCX, NCDEX, COMEX and IIBX plus new equity and currency derivatives verticals and subsidiaries in Dubai and Mauritius. In response to FY 2025-26 scaling the Company had to upgrade real-time position monitoring, improve reconciliation of simultaneous positions across multiple exchanges, tighten cross-border documentation and redraw responsibilities between trading, settlement and treasury teams — indicating the control burden grows with scale.
- Trade-policy and tariff dependence of the jewellery/export channel — US reciprocal tariffs of 50% on most Indian goods including gems and jewellery from August 2025 rendered Indian jewellery less competitive; relief to 18% came only in February 2026 and further reduction for gems and diamonds depends on finalisation of an Interim Agreement, leaving the export channel exposed to policy reversal.

business.body: AEL participates in commodity derivatives, bullion, agricultural commodities, base metals, equity derivatives and currency derivatives, operating simultaneously in the financial and physical markets — risk management across MCX, NCDEX, COMEX and the India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX) at GIFT City on one side, and physical procurement spanning India's agricultural heartlands, global bullion channels and structured delivery infrastructure on the other. Key commodity trades are in agricultural commodities such as coriander, guar seed and guar gum, precious metals such as gold and silver bar, precious stones such as diamond, and derivatives listed on recognised Indian exchanges; the Company describes itself as a low-margin, high-velocity trading business serving a wide spectrum of commodity clients and counterparties. Through wholly owned subsidiary Abans Jewels Limited it also operates a predominantly B2B premium jewellery business — a registered jeweller with associations with major bullion bankers that trades precious and base metals and manufactures precious/semi-precious stone studded gold and diamond jewellery for high-net-worth retailers, premium stores and discerning individual clients. The Company is listed on BSE and MSEI and operates through wholly owned subsidiaries in Dubai (UAE), Mauritius and India.

outlook.body:
- Protect and strengthen the core trading franchise with sharper focus on risk-adjusted profitability rather than volume alone (CEO's stated priority for FY 2026-27)
- Improve capital and working-capital efficiency by aligning exposures, funding and inventory more closely with opportunity and liquidity
- Deepen relationships with credible suppliers, customers, financial institutions and strategic partners across domestic and international markets
- Use technology, automation and data-driven intelligence to strengthen execution, controls and management visibility — creating timely, decision-ready information across trading, treasury, risk, finance and compliance and reducing manual dependencies
- Build complementary, scalable business opportunities adjacent to existing capabilities without compromising balance-sheet discipline
- Maintain governance, compliance and responsible conduct as non-negotiable foundations, with a strengthened risk architecture — clearer risk limits, improved management information, faster escalation of exceptions and greater visibility into liquidity and counterparty exposures
- Institutionalise discipline rather than depend on individual judgement, in what management describes as a low-margin, high-velocity business where small improvements in risk selection, funding efficiency and execution quality materially improve outcomes
- Operate simultaneously across the financial and physical commodity markets — physical procurement networks paired with derivative hedging across MCX, NCDEX, COMEX and IIBX — as the stated source of competitive advantage
- Leverage GIFT City institutional standing: Qualified Jeweller and TRQ Holder status (through Abans Jewels Limited) for duty-concessional gold imports via IIBX under the India-UAE CEPA regime, described as an early-mover structural procurement cost advantage over peers reliant on traditional nominated bank channels
- Extend the intelligence-led trading model beyond commodities into equity, equity derivatives and currency derivatives markets
- Pursue growth selectively and allocate resources where the Company has a genuine right to win, with decisions anchored in capital preservation, cash generation and sustainable returns
- Keep the jewellery business (AJL) focused on the premium domestic B2B segment, where handcrafted design-led offerings and trusted supply relationships serve high-net-worth retailers and premium stores
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: AEL is asset-light and its expansion during FY 2025-26 was market-access, vertical and platform build-out rather than physical plant. The Company formally expanded its participation into equity, equity derivatives and currency derivatives markets, extending its intelligence-led trading model beyond commodities into India's broader financial markets. Derivative and risk-management capability was deepened across MCX, NCDEX, COMEX and the India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX) at GIFT City, and the physical footprint spans India's agricultural heartlands, global bullion procurement channels and structured delivery infrastructure. Institutional positioning at GIFT City is carried through Abans Jewels Limited, which holds Qualified Jeweller and Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ) status at IIBX, enabling duty-concessional gold imports under the India-UAE CEPA regime formalised by the IFSCA framework circular of October 2025. The Company operates through wholly owned subsidiaries in Dubai (UAE), Mauritius and India; as on March 31, 2026 it has two subsidiaries and one step-down subsidiary and no associates or joint ventures. A planned structural simplification was reversed: the Scheme of Amalgamation of Abans Jewels Limited into Abans Enterprises Limited, approved on November 8, 2024, was withdrawn because, in view of evolving business and market dynamics, the expected benefits were not sufficiently demonstrable. Organisational capacity was expanded with headcount rising to 104 permanent employees as of March 31, 2026 from 68 a year earlier, reflecting expansion in trading, risk management, technology and compliance functions. Internal systems were strengthened in four ways during the year: real-time monitoring upgraded to flag unusual positions instantly, reconciliation improved for simultaneous positions across multiple exchanges, cross-border documentation tightened, and responsibilities between trading, settlement and treasury teams reviewed and updated. Forward-looking build-out remains at the intention stage: the CEO describes strengthening governance and risk architecture (clearer risk limits, improved management information, faster escalation of exceptions) and investing in technology and data to create decision-ready information across trading, treasury, risk, finance and compliance, while management states the lending vertical requires a capital scale-up that internal accruals alone may not sustain. No rupee capex quantum, project commissioning timeline or installed capacity is disclosed in this material.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Management states that for gold and silver the fundamentals remain supportive into FY 2026-27, and that India's bullion market outlook remains compelling
- Record-high gold and silver prices are expected to moderate jewellery volumes, while investment demand is likely to remain strong — driven by global uncertainty from the Middle East conflict, the RBI's continued accumulation of gold, and growing retail familiarity with bullion as an asset class
- The World Gold Council projects India's gold consumption in the range of 750-850 tonnes for FY 2026-27 (third-party projection)
- Silver demand is expected to remain robust, supported by India's solar manufacturing ambitions (the country targeting 500 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030) and its rapidly growing electronics sector; silver is described as undergoing structural transformation from a monetary metal to an essential industrial commodity, with a sixth consecutive year of structural supply deficit
- Management says that with integrated physical and derivative bullion capabilities and institutional presence in GIFT City, this environment represents a strong strategic fit for AEL
- Deepening of IIBX at GIFT City is cited as a structural tailwind — SBI became the first public sector bank to execute a gold trade on IIBX as a Special Category Client, and the IFSCA framework circular of October 2025 formalised the India-UAE CEPA Tariff Rate Quota regime
- Commodity-market formalisation is a stated opportunity: SEBI has broadened participation by FPIs, AIFs, PMS and mutual funds in commodity derivatives, and electricity futures approval deepens institutional liquidity on MCX and NCDEX, benefiting established participants
- US-India trade de-escalation — the reduction of US tariffs on Indian goods from 50% to 18% effective February 2026 — improves the economics of export-oriented businesses including jewellery and gems, with the Interim Agreement framework potentially reducing tariffs on gems and diamonds specifically; the full benefit is expected to be felt primarily in FY 2026-27
- The domestic premium and luxury jewellery segment is expected to grow, supported by India's expanding high-net-worth population and the enduring cultural significance of gold; the premium/bespoke segment showed greater resilience against commodity price volatility than mass-market and export segments
- Energy is the named near-term watch point: the Strait of Hormuz disruption and expiry of the US waiver on Russian crude could drive imported inflation, weaken the rupee and force the RBI to pause its easing cycle, while higher oil prices raise operating costs for commodity transportation, storage and processing across AEL's supply chain
- Volatility itself is framed as a driver — management states markets may remain volatile but volatility also creates opportunity for organisations that possess liquidity, intelligence, relationships and discipline
- Management acknowledges trading scale expanded while profitability remained under pressure, and says the coming year will be about converting resilience into performance
- Equity derivatives volumes stabilised at more sustainable levels after SEBI's FY 2024-25 tightening (larger minimum contract sizes, reduced weekly expiries), with a greater share of activity from hedgers and institutional participants; commodity derivatives by contrast saw exceptional activity and record notional bullion turnover on MCX

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Management states that for gold and silver the fundamentals remain supportive into FY 2026-27, and that India's bullion market outlook remains compelling
- Record-high gold and silver prices are expected to moderate jewellery volumes, while investment demand is likely to remain strong — driven by global uncertainty from the Middle East conflict, the RBI's continued accumulation of gold, and growing retail familiarity with bullion as an asset class
- The World Gold Council projects India's gold consumption in the range of 750-850 tonnes for FY 2026-27 (third-party projection)
- Silver demand is expected to remain robust, supported by India's solar manufacturing ambitions (the country targeting 500 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030) and its rapidly growing electronics sector; silver is described as undergoing structural transformation from a monetary metal to an essential industrial commodity, with a sixth consecutive year of structural supply deficit
- Management says that with integrated physical and derivative bullion capabilities and institutional presence in GIFT City, this environment represents a strong strategic fit for AEL
- Deepening of IIBX at GIFT City is cited as a structural tailwind — SBI became the first public sector bank to execute a gold trade on IIBX as a Special Category Client, and the IFSCA framework circular of October 2025 formalised the India-UAE CEPA Tariff Rate Quota regime
- Commodity-market formalisation is a stated opportunity: SEBI has broadened participation by FPIs, AIFs, PMS and mutual funds in commodity derivatives, and electricity futures approval deepens institutional liquidity on MCX and NCDEX, benefiting established participants
- US-India trade de-escalation — the reduction of US tariffs on Indian goods from 50% to 18% effective February 2026 — improves the economics of export-oriented businesses including jewellery and gems, with the Interim Agreement framework potentially reducing tariffs on gems and diamonds specifically; the full benefit is expected to be felt primarily in FY 2026-27
- The domestic premium and luxury jewellery segment is expected to grow, supported by India's expanding high-net-worth population and the enduring cultural significance of gold; the premium/bespoke segment showed greater resilience against commodity price volatility than mass-market and export segments
- Energy is the named near-term watch point: the Strait of Hormuz disruption and expiry of the US waiver on Russian crude could drive imported inflation, weaken the rupee and force the RBI to pause its easing cycle, while higher oil prices raise operating costs for commodity transportation, storage and processing across AEL's supply chain
- Volatility itself is framed as a driver — management states markets may remain volatile but volatility also creates opportunity for organisations that possess liquidity, intelligence, relationships and discipline
- Management acknowledges trading scale expanded while profitability remained under pressure, and says the coming year will be about converting resilience into performance
- Equity derivatives volumes stabilised at more sustainable levels after SEBI's FY 2024-25 tightening (larger minimum contract sizes, reduced weekly expiries), with a greater share of activity from hedgers and institutional participants; commodity derivatives by contrast saw exceptional activity and record notional bullion turnover on MCX

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Protect and strengthen the core trading franchise with sharper focus on risk-adjusted profitability rather than volume alone (CEO's stated priority for FY 2026-27)
- Improve capital and working-capital efficiency by aligning exposures, funding and inventory more closely with opportunity and liquidity
- Deepen relationships with credible suppliers, customers, financial institutions and strategic partners across domestic and international markets
- Use technology, automation and data-driven intelligence to strengthen execution, controls and management visibility — creating timely, decision-ready information across trading, treasury, risk, finance and compliance and reducing manual dependencies
- Build complementary, scalable business opportunities adjacent to existing capabilities without compromising balance-sheet discipline
- Maintain governance, compliance and responsible conduct as non-negotiable foundations, with a strengthened risk architecture — clearer risk limits, improved management information, faster escalation of exceptions and greater visibility into liquidity and counterparty exposures
- Institutionalise discipline rather than depend on individual judgement, in what management describes as a low-margin, high-velocity business where small improvements in risk selection, funding efficiency and execution quality materially improve outcomes
- Operate simultaneously across the financial and physical commodity markets — physical procurement networks paired with derivative hedging across MCX, NCDEX, COMEX and IIBX — as the stated source of competitive advantage
- Leverage GIFT City institutional standing: Qualified Jeweller and TRQ Holder status (through Abans Jewels Limited) for duty-concessional gold imports via IIBX under the India-UAE CEPA regime, described as an early-mover structural procurement cost advantage over peers reliant on traditional nominated bank channels
- Extend the intelligence-led trading model beyond commodities into equity, equity derivatives and currency derivatives markets
- Pursue growth selectively and allocate resources where the Company has a genuine right to win, with decisions anchored in capital preservation, cash generation and sustainable returns
- Keep the jewellery business (AJL) focused on the premium domestic B2B segment, where handcrafted design-led offerings and trusted supply relationships serve high-net-worth retailers and premium stores

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: AEL is asset-light and its expansion during FY 2025-26 was market-access, vertical and platform build-out rather than physical plant. The Company formally expanded its participation into equity, equity derivatives and currency derivatives markets, extending its intelligence-led trading model beyond commodities into India's broader financial markets. Derivative and risk-management capability was deepened across MCX, NCDEX, COMEX and the India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX) at GIFT City, and the physical footprint spans India's agricultural heartlands, global bullion procurement channels and structured delivery infrastructure. Institutional positioning at GIFT City is carried through Abans Jewels Limited, which holds Qualified Jeweller and Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ) status at IIBX, enabling duty-concessional gold imports under the India-UAE CEPA regime formalised by the IFSCA framework circular of October 2025. The Company operates through wholly owned subsidiaries in Dubai (UAE), Mauritius and India; as on March 31, 2026 it has two subsidiaries and one step-down subsidiary and no associates or joint ventures. A planned structural simplification was reversed: the Scheme of Amalgamation of Abans Jewels Limited into Abans Enterprises Limited, approved on November 8, 2024, was withdrawn because, in view of evolving business and market dynamics, the expected benefits were not sufficiently demonstrable. Organisational capacity was expanded with headcount rising to 104 permanent employees as of March 31, 2026 from 68 a year earlier, reflecting expansion in trading, risk management, technology and compliance functions. Internal systems were strengthened in four ways during the year: real-time monitoring upgraded to flag unusual positions instantly, reconciliation improved for simultaneous positions across multiple exchanges, cross-border documentation tightened, and responsibilities between trading, settlement and treasury teams reviewed and updated. Forward-looking build-out remains at the intention stage: the CEO describes strengthening governance and risk architecture (clearer risk limits, improved management information, faster escalation of exceptions) and investing in technology and data to create decision-ready information across trading, treasury, risk, finance and compliance, while management states the lending vertical requires a capital scale-up that internal accruals alone may not sustain. No rupee capex quantum, project commissioning timeline or installed capacity is disclosed in this material.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Dual financial-and-physical capability: management identifies the ability to operate simultaneously across derivatives markets (MCX, NCDEX, COMEX, IIBX) and physical procurement/delivery infrastructure as its core competitive advantage in a volatile market
- Structural procurement cost advantage: GIFT City Qualified Jeweller status and India-UAE CEPA Tariff Rate Quota access enable duty-concessional gold imports through IIBX, which the Company describes as a cost advantage over peers reliant on traditional nominated bank channels
- Early-mover institutional position at IIBX as India's bullion import architecture formalises, which management says creates lasting structural value as SBI and other PSUs join as participants
- Counterparty risk record: the Company states it navigated the most volatile precious metals environment in a generation without a single counterparty default, with every transaction fully hedged and physically backed
- Approved risk-management mechanism with strict limits on maximum exposure, stop loss and maximum deal size, hedging via exchange-traded futures and options; 100% of disclosed domestic agri-commodity exposures (coriander, guar gum, guar seeds) were hedged through exchange derivatives
- Established trading relationships: trusted position across India's bullion corridors, and for AJL, associations with major bullion bankers plus a strong net worth and robust banking relationships that support the Group's trading fund-raising requirements
- Diversified portfolio across agri commodities, bullion, base metals, derivatives, equity markets and bespoke jewellery, reducing reliance on any single market segment
- Design-led premium jewellery positioning: handcrafted designs and trusted supply relationships in the premium/bespoke segment, where management says design innovation, artisan craftsmanship and brand trust command a price premium with greater resilience to commodity price volatility
- Board independence: over fifty percent of the Board comprises Independent Directors, including one Woman Independent Director, and an independent internal audit firm reports directly to the Audit Committee
- A decade of disciplined execution and institutional relationship-building under current management since 2015 (management's own characterisation)

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Bullion price concentration risk — Management flags that bullion trading constitutes the substantial majority of AEL's revenues, so a sustained correction in precious metals prices or spread compression could disproportionately impact financial performance. This is a structural single-commodity concentration, not a cyclical one.
- Working capital intensity at scale — Listed as a threat: margin management, collateral management and reconciliation demands are materially different from two years prior following the step-up in trading scale, and technology and treasury systems must continue to scale commensurately.
- Treasury and risk-management infrastructure must scale with volumes — The MD&A 'Risk and Concerns' section states the scale of treasury operations requires continued investment in risk management infrastructure as volumes compound — an ongoing cost and operational-failure exposure tied to growth.
- Lending vertical undercapitalised relative to the opportunity — Management states the lending vertical requires capital scale-up to capture the full opportunity and that internal accruals alone may not sustain the target growth rate — implying a dependence on external capital.
- Middle East conflict — energy and macro risk — The Strait of Hormuz disruption removes a significant share of global crude supply and the US waiver for Russian crude purchases expired April 11, 2026. Management warns this could drive imported inflation, weaken the rupee and force the RBI to pause its easing cycle, while higher oil prices raise operating costs for commodity transportation, storage and processing across AEL's supply chain.
- Extreme commodity price volatility and intraday dislocation — FY 2025-26 saw gold and silver at generational highs and one of the most violent intraday reversals in modern commodity history (silver, December 29, 2025). Management cites the flash crash as demonstrating the risks of volatile commodity markets; the derivatives desk operated in the most demanding environment in the Company's history.
- Multi-exchange, cross-border operational and control complexity — Operations span MCX, NCDEX, COMEX and IIBX plus new equity and currency derivatives verticals and subsidiaries in Dubai and Mauritius. In response to FY 2025-26 scaling the Company had to upgrade real-time position monitoring, improve reconciliation of simultaneous positions across multiple exchanges, tighten cross-border documentation and redraw responsibilities between trading, settlement and treasury teams — indicating the control burden grows with scale.
- Trade-policy and tariff dependence of the jewellery/export channel — US reciprocal tariffs of 50% on most Indian goods including gems and jewellery from August 2025 rendered Indian jewellery less competitive; relief to 18% came only in February 2026 and further reduction for gems and diamonds depends on finalisation of an Interim Agreement, leaving the export channel exposed to policy reversal.
